Title: Will your AI turn backers away? Evidence from Kickstarter's AI-use disclosure policy
Authors: Sonika Singhal, Yeongin Kim, Seonjun Kang, Victoria Yoon
Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping how creative work is produced, raising new questions about authenticity, originality, and human effort in entrepreneurial settings. We examine how platform-mandated AI-use disclosure is associated with crowdfunding outcomes, using Kickstarter’s 2023 disclosure policy and a dataset of over 63,000 campaigns launched between 2022 and 2024. Drawing on signaling theory, we argue that an AI-use label functions as a platform-governed cue that backers may interpret as signaling reduced human effort, potentially shaping how they evaluate creators and campaigns. Empirically, we find that AI-use disclosure is associated with a significantly lower likelihood of campaign success, with this negative association concentrated in reduced backer participation. The disclosure penalty is weaker when campaign descriptions are more subjective and easier to read, but stronger in technology-oriented campaigns where human expertise and originality are especially salient. It is also weaker for creators with stronger prior track records. Our findings identify AI-use disclosure as a novel platform-governed signal in crowdfunding, contribute to research on how platform-designed information environments shape user evaluations, and highlight potential unintended consequences of AI transparency requirements for platform design and policy.

Title: The rise of AI-enabled new product ideation: End of innovation crowdsourcing?
Authors: Heeseung Lee, Likoebe Maruping
Abstract: Innovation crowdsourcing has been a critical source of creativity for new product development, leveraging diverse human perspectives and tacit knowledge to generate novel ideas. The rapid rise of generative AI, with capabilities approaching human-like creativity, challenges the traditional value of human crowdsourcing, prompting firms to reconsider how they source innovative ideas. Drawing on von Hippel's theory of user innovation and the concept of knowledge stickiness, we theorize how AI-conceivable and crowd-conceivable features differ in their impact on needs specification and needs fulfillment, and identify two boundary conditions that shape GenAI's relative effectiveness. Our empirical findings reveal that AI-conceivable features positively influence both needs specification and needs fulfillment, but their impacts are contingent. Technical complexity amplifies the positive effect of AI-conceivability on needs specification, reflecting GenAI's advantage in synthesizing explicit technical knowledge. In contrast, pain point specificity attenuates the positive effect of AI-conceivability on needs fulfillment, suggesting GenAI's limitations in accessing the tacit, embodied knowledge that underpins user pain point solutions. These findings advance a contingency-based understanding of GenAI's role in innovation crowdsourcing and offer guidance for firms seeking to integrate AI-enabled and human-driven ideation.

Title: An AI-enabled decision support system for evidence-based last-mile delivery authentication: design and pilot implementation
Authors: D. Prithvirajan, M. Mathirajan
Abstract: Reliable last-mile delivery of essential commodities continues to face significant operational challenges arising from delivery disputes, black-market diversion, and limited post-delivery auditability. Existing delivery authentication mechanisms primarily rely on acknowledgements such as signatures and one-time passwords, which provide limited independent evidence that a delivery has physically occurred. To address this challenge, this study develops and pilots an AI-enabled Decision Support System (DSS) for evidence-based delivery authentication in LPG cylinder distribution. The proposed DSS integrates an image verification module and a geolocation verification module and is deployed as a Progressive Web Application. The DSS automatically authenticates delivery events and generates multimodal operational evidence to support post-delivery auditing. The system was deployed under live field conditions across LPG distribution operations in Chennai and Kumbakonam, India. Pilot results demonstrated the practical feasibility of the DSS under diverse delivery scenarios and environmental conditions, with delivery authentication typically completed within a few seconds during routine field operations and without requiring specialised infrastructure, customer participation, or significant additional operational effort. This study contributes to the DSS literature by demonstrating how lightweight mobile-integrated AI technologies can be embedded within execution-level last-mile operations to strengthen accountability, operational visibility, and post-delivery auditability.

Title: Advancing personalized healthcare for elderly individuals through AI-enhanced preventive disease risk stratification decision
Authors: Tsung-Hsing Chen, Chia-Yu Lai, Chieh Lee, Jen Yu, Ta-Sen Yeh
Abstract: Personalized long-term care (LTC) has become an emerging healthcare policy priority in response to the rapidly aging population worldwide. LTC, especially in the prevention and early detection of precancerous conditions, plays a crucial role in reducing mortality rates and alleviating the financial burden on individuals and healthcare institutions. This study develops an LTC risk stratification artifact that does not rely on advanced examinations. Such a design categorizes individuals into risk groups using artificial intelligence (AI) methods with a parameter selection process and supports non-communicable disease prevention. The AI-Enhanced Decision Support System (AIEDSS), developed by conducting action design research (ADR) and aligned with Sustainable Development Goal 3 (SDG 3), aims to reduce healthcare costs while improving health outcomes for elderly populations. We evaluate the artifact using annual healthcare checkup data from Chang Gung Memorial Hospital (CGMH), demonstrating its effectiveness in disease risk stratification. The efficacy of AIEDSS is demonstrated by a more than 97% true-positive rate (sensitivity) in identifying elderly individuals with gallstones and 80% sensitivity in identifying adenoma. In addition, the modeling approach is well received by physicians in both quantitative and qualitative evaluations. This study presents the AIEDSS as a sociotechnical artifact, integrating an advanced AI model with physician-guided design to support disease diagnostic decision-making in personalized LTC and to enhance the efficiency, affordability, and sustainability of healthcare services.

Title: Explainable AI model for predicting customer service communication effectiveness: A computational design science approach
Authors: Xin Liu, Lin Jia, Gemin Liang, Yifan Yu
Abstract: Effective communication between customer service representatives (CSRs) and customers is essential for maintaining customer relationships and improving operational performance. Although firms have increasingly used AI technologies to evaluate customer service communication effectiveness, existing approaches primarily rely on dialogue texts while ignoring sequential communication strategies that reveal CSRs' underlying intentions. Furthermore, communication strategies are often quantified through manual coding, limiting scalability and explainability. Consequently, it remains unclear how individual strategies and their combinations contribute to AI-based predictions of communication effectiveness. Following the Computational Design Science research paradigm and Aristotle's Rhetoric Theory, this study proposes an explainable customer service communication effectiveness prediction model with text-strategy dual input based on the Transformer Encoder architecture (ExTSdiT). To enable automated strategy quantification, we design few-shot Chain-of-Thought prompts to guide large language models in annotating communication strategy labels from CSR utterances. Customized model explainability techniques are further employed to analyze the effects of individual strategies and their combinations at the dialogue-turn level. The framework is evaluated on a large-scale real-world customer service call dataset. Results show that the proposed model outperforms benchmark methods across multiple metrics and exhibits robust performance in ablation and stability analyses. The explainability results can support customer service communication quality inspection, and facilitate data-driven customer service training.

Title: Designing humanoid agents for economic decision-making with LLMs: A framework based on cognitive architecture and dual-process theory
Authors: Liming Zhao, Haichao Zheng, Bin Zhu, Chao Liu
Abstract: Humanoid agents are intelligent entities designed to think and behave in ways that resemble human cognition and actions. Despite their growing significance in economic decision-making studies, there is a lack of comprehensive theoretical frameworks to guide the design of such agents. Powered by large language models (LLMs), this paper addresses this gap by proposing a framework that integrates cognitive architecture and dual-process theory. Following the Design Science Research methodology, we develop humanoid agents based on the proposed framework and evaluate their performance using three metrics: the Turing Test, Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the decision distributions of the agents and humans in classic economic decision-making games, and the Confusion Matrix-derived Metrics. The findings show that humanoid agents designed using the proposed framework exhibit a higher degree of human-like behaviors than baseline agents. This paper contributes to the design of humanoid agents and the development of cognitive architecture in the following ways. First, it introduces a novel framework for designing humanoid agents in economic decision-making, integrating cognitive architecture and dual-process theory. Second, it incorporates a reasoning module based on dual-process theory into traditional cognitive architecture, empowered by LLMs, thereby expanding the design and application potential of cognitive architecture.

Title: Exploring the involuntary and excessive use of mobile instant messaging for work-related purposes: A triangulated mixed-methods investigation
Authors: Tingting Hou, Ping Ding, Keke Hou, Yifeng Ruan, Xin (Robert) Luo
Abstract: While mobile instant messaging (MIM) has become increasingly ubiquitous in professional settings, its psychological implications remain underexplored. Grounded in Cognitive Load Theory and the stressor-strain-outcome framework, the present study examines how involuntary use and excessive use of MIM are associated with social media fatigue and switching intention. Employing a three-stage mixed-methods design comprising an initial qualitative exploration, a quantitative study, and a qualitative follow-up, this study identifies four context-specific psychological states: privacy concerns, information overload, impaired autonomy, and work-to-life conflict. The findings reveal that these psychological states underlie the associations of both excessive and involuntary MIM use with user fatigue and switching intention. These insights illuminate the nature of technology-induced digital stressors in contemporary work environments.

Title: Confirmation or overload? The nonlinear impact of topic-extension on revisiting consultation in online healthcare
Authors: Jiantong Zhang, Yuting Zhang, Binhua Ye, Yushan Guo
Abstract: Sustaining patient engagement remains a central challenge for online health communities (OHCs). This study examines how physicians' topic-extension responses—the proactive provision of clinically relevant information beyond patients' explicitly stated inquiries—shape revisiting consultation and through which mechanisms. Using a multimethod design, Study 1 analyzes physician-period consultation data from a leading OHC and reveals an inverted U-shaped relationship between topic-extension and aggregate revisiting consultation: moderate extension increases revisiting, whereas excessive extension reduces it. This nonlinear relationship becomes flatter when physicians serve patient populations with higher health literacy. Study 2 employs a scenario-based experiment to establish causality and unpack the underlying psychological process. The results show that increasing topic-extension from a low to a moderate level enhances revisiting intention through greater expectation confirmation, whereas increasing it from a moderate to an excessive level reduces revisiting intention through heightened perceived cognitive load. Together, the findings demonstrate that the effectiveness of topic-extension responses depends on both the extent and the characteristics of the patient population and provide important implications for optimizing online physician–patient communication.

Title: TORA: Topic-based rule affinity for content moderation in social media communities
Authors: Kanlun Wang, Zhe Fu, Wangjiaxuan Xin, Kevin Hanson, Lina Zhou
Abstract: While social media platforms enable the exchange of information and experiences across online communities, their extensive connectivity simultaneously accelerates the dissemination of misleading and potentially harmful content. Content moderation serves as a crucial mechanism for curbing such dissemination, with community rules playing a central role in guiding moderation decisions. Despite significant advances in automated content moderation, the explicit incorporation of community rules into model design remains rare. Among the different levels of social aggregation where community rules operate, macro norms establish standardized governance principles to ensure consistency across communities; however, they remain largely overlooked in automated content moderation research. To address these gaps, we propose TOpic-based Rule Affinity (TORA), a content moderation framework that draws on and adapts polycentric governance theory, algorithmic governance theory, and sociotechnical systems theory to incorporate rules from heterogeneous communities into moderation. Following the design science paradigm, TORA introduces two novel design artifacts: topic-based macro norms, which use Large Language Models (LLMs) to capture and standardize rules across diverse communities, and a topic-based rule affinity measure, which quantifies the relationship between user-generated content and those norms. We implement and evaluate TORA using data collected from multiple social media communities. Empirical results show that the framework consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baseline models, and each of its two key design artifacts contributes significantly to improved performance. These findings make significant theoretical and design contributions and have implications for improving societal outcomes by enabling more interpretable and transparent content moderation and supporting fairness and justice in online governance.

Title: Editorial Board
AI advice and human metacognition
Authors: Leily Soleimanof, Derrick Neufeld
Abstract: Although organizations increasingly rely on artificial intelligence (AI) to support decision making, research consistently finds that decision makers exhibit varied responses to algorithmic advice. While prior research has examined when users are more likely to accept or reject AI advice, little is known about the cognitive factors associated with these responses or the broader psychological consequences of working with AI. Drawing on metacognition theory, this study explores how individuals monitor and revise their judgments when confronted with algorithmic advice in a behavioral experiment with 440 participants. The results indicate that metacognitive estimates of confidence are strongly associated with responses to algorithmic advice. However, individual differences in metacognitive sensitivity shape how consistently they rely on confidence when responding to AI advice. Specifically, when metacognitive sensitivity is low, confidence judgments are based on noisy internal states, which, in turn, lead to inconsistent patterns of advice-taking. We also find that exposure to contradictory AI advice is associated with lower retrospective confidence in individuals' subsequent decisions. This loss of confidence is more pronounced when individuals reject the AI advice, highlighting a hidden psychological cost of advice rejection. These findings contribute to the growing body of information systems (IS) research on algorithmic advice-taking by demonstrating that effective human-AI collaboration requires not only improvements in system design but also fostering users' metacognitive sensitivity.

Title: Toward explainable clinical decision support for irregular and incomplete ICU EHRs: An observation-aware multi-level attention model
Authors: Kaibo Zhu, Xuan Wei, Xiuxian Wang, Na Geng
Abstract: Intensive care units (ICUs) are high-acuity environments where patient conditions evolve rapidly and require continuous monitoring. These settings generate rich, high-frequency electronic health records (EHRs), offering critical opportunities for data-driven decision support. However, ICU EHRs are characterized by irregular sampling, widespread missingness, and a heterogeneous structure. These characteristics hinder the development of reliable and interpretable machine learning models—two qualities essential for safe clinical deployment. This study proposes MMAEM (Masked Multi-level Attention Encoding Model), an observation-aware clinical decision support model that integrates static demographic information with dynamic multivariate time series through a hybrid encoder architecture. The approach employs an explicit masking strategy to learn directly from sparse and irregular sequences without imputing unobserved values. Moreover, it incorporates a multi-level attention mechanism, spanning the feature-, timestep-, and trend-level dimensions. This mechanism is designed to provide structured, temporally resolved explanatory signals grounded in observed clinical data and to improve the transparency of model output in irregular ICU time series. Using real-world ICU data, we evaluate the model in an early sepsis prediction case study and show that enhanced transparency can be achieved without compromising predictive performance. By aligning algorithmic innovation with the transparency requirements of clinical practice, this work advances the development of explainable predictive models and supports their practical adoption in ICU decision support systems.

Title: TRACE: Transaction representation learning for large-scale Ethereum phishing detection under limited labels
Authors: Hojun Kang, Sang-Gun Lee
Abstract: Ethereum phishing detection is a decision-support problem: blockchain risk analysts must prioritize suspicious addresses under severe label scarcity and bounded review capacity. We present TRACE, a two-stage decision-support artifact that constructs dense Ethereum address graphs from Etherscan transaction records, pre-trains an edge-aware encoder with graph contrastive learning, and adapts it with validation-based threshold calibration and explanation analysis for reviewable phishing screening. Rather than proposing new learning primitives, the contribution is a domain-grounded configuration whose individual design choices are non-obvious for dense, heavy-tailed transaction graphs and whose benefit grows with graph scale. Across five graphs from 30,000 to 149,930 addresses, six label ratios, eight baselines, and five random seeds, TRACE achieves the best overall mean performance (F1 0.5094; AUC 0.9365). Component ablations, paired significance tests, precision–recall (AUPRC) reporting, and prevalence-sensitivity experiments down to sub-1% phishing rates confirm that each design element contributes and that the advantage is stable under realistic class imbalance. Performance improves with graph scale, reaching F1 0.6720 and AUC 0.9730 on D150k under full labels, and a smaller pre-training graph transfers to a larger target (F1 0.5670). The artifact logic generalizes to other scarce-label, interaction-rich risk-screening settings beyond Ethereum.

Title: Understanding individual online social exclusion: Conceptualization, scale development, and validation
Authors: Bryan Iwata Hammer, Andy Luse, Caleb Krieger, Gabriel Bahr, Forough Nasirpouri Shadbad
Abstract: Despite an increase in research on social exclusion, a consistent definition and measure is lacking, especially for online and virtual environments. Additionally, previous measures cannot account for inconsistencies in the literature, such as social exclusion's relationship with trust and social factors. In this research, we present a review of the literature, clarify the conceptualization, and provide a definition. Using a student sample and another more general population, we develop a two-dimensional scale. First, we use focus groups to develop new survey items, then rely on subject-matter experts to assess content validity. After developing measurement items, an exploratory analysis for grouping the items and confirmatory analysis for validating the measure was conducted, followed by group & predictive analyses to further validate the measure. The new scale reliably and validly appraises individual online social exclusion. The scale resolves inconsistencies from the literature, showing it to be more discerning than previous operationalizations.

Title: ECS-VTabNet: An interpretable federated learning approach for imbalanced credit classification
Authors: Zhongyi Wang, Eric W.T. Ngai, Zhang Wen, Yuhang Tian, Sihan Li
Abstract: Credit classification, which aims to characterize user profiles and accurately predict default risks, is critical for financial risk management. Although centralized models trained on directly aggregated multi-source data can achieve strong performance, they often disregard data privacy, class imbalance, and model interpretability. To address these gaps, we propose an example-dependent cost-sensitive vertical TabNet (ECS-VTabNet), a novel framework for privacy-preserving collaborative credit classification. The proposed framework integrates vertical federated learning with an attentive interpretable model (i.e., TabNet) and an example-dependent cost-sensitive (ECS) loss function. Our approach enables multiple institutions to collaboratively build a highly accurate credit scoring model without sharing raw data. The ECS mechanism aligns the model with business objectives by minimizing financial losses, and TabNet's inherent architecture provides transparent feature importance. Experimental results on two public credit datasets show that ECS-VTabNet outperforms existing federated and centralized methods in managing imbalanced data and providing interpretable predictions while avoiding raw data exchange under the honest-but-curious assumption. This work provides a practical solution for financial institutions seeking to build robust, compliant, and collaborative risk assessment models without centralizing sensitive client data.

Title: Identifying suspicious online reviews of telemedicine applications based on homophily principle and social presence theory
Authors: Chengfei Wang, Wenting (Kayla) Jiang, Ashish Gupta, Han Li
Abstract: Amid the growing threat of fake reviews, manipulated reviews of telemedicine applications (hereafter: apps) can mislead patients into choosing ineffective telemedicine services, compromising their well-being. Detecting suspicious reviews of telemedicine apps is crucial for safe services. However, it is constrained by the scarcity of domain-specific, annotated data. To overcome this challenge, we integrate the homophily principle and social presence theory to develop a dual-pronged approach to identifying app-level clusters exhibiting suspicious aggregate review patterns that warrant targeted investigation. The first prong is based on the homophily principle and employs a novel community-detection-based approach to generate communities of telemedicine apps. The second prong uses network and text analytics to compare clusters to identify those containing suspicious reviews. We validated our double-pronged approach on 166 telemedicine apps from the Google Play Store. In line with social presence theory and the deception detection literature, reviews in the suspicious cluster exhibited low social presence, with more formal, detached, mechanical, and superficial content, and a lack of detailed personal disclosure and in-depth cognitive reasoning. This study has important implications for the literature on suspicious review identification and for the practical design of systems that combat review manipulation in domains lacking high-quality annotated data.

Title: A decision support framework for privacy risk assessment on social media through automated personally identifiable information detection
Authors: Fangyu Lin, Yizhi Liu, Weifeng Li, Reza Ebrahimi, Hsinchun Chen
Abstract: Personally Identifiable Information (PII) exposure on social media creates serious privacy risks, including identity theft and targeted scams, yet users and platforms lack effective tools to detect and assess such exposures in a timely manner. This study adopts a computational design science approach and proposes a decision support framework for social media privacy risk assessment, with automated PII extraction at its core. We develop MCA-PIIE, a deep learning–based PII extraction model that combines deep transfer learning with multi-context attention to address limited labeled data and capture semantic, syntactic, and PII-indicative cues in informal social media text. The framework is evaluated against state-of-the-art PII extraction methods using well-established public datasets and a curated Twitter ground-truth dataset. The results show that MCA-PIIE achieves an F1 of 72.34% on social media data, outperforming from-scratch and prompt-based baselines and matching the accuracy of a QLoRA fine-tuned 8B language model while using roughly 400 times fewer parameters. An exploratory user study examines how the proposed framework helps users identify PII exposure on social media and how their privacy-protection decisions align with the system-assessed risk levels. This study contributes a decision support perspective to social media privacy analytics and offers design insights for privacy-aware information systems.

Title: Concerto of rhetoric and images: The effect of multimodal aesthetics on customers' booking intentions in P2P accommodation
Authors: Haiwang Liu, Xiaoyun Han, Limin Xiao
Abstract: Despite the importance of aesthetics in peer-to-peer (P2P) accommodation, prior studies have neither integrated rhetoric into the multimodal information framework nor examined the synergistic or antagonistic effects between rhetoric aesthetics and image aesthetics. To address this gap, this study employs text mining and image detection techniques to operationalize aesthetics as rhetoric aesthetics and image aesthetics, with the latter further comprising cover image aesthetics and sleep space image aesthetics. Based on aesthetic arousal theory, this study uses secondary data from 20,144 Airbnb listings to construct econometric models and conducts four scenario-based experiments. The results indicate that rhetoric aesthetics has an inverted U-shaped effect on customers' booking intentions, mediated by aesthetic pleasure—that is, rhetoric aesthetics exerts an inverted U-shaped effect on aesthetic pleasure, which in turn positively influences customers' booking intentions. Cover image aesthetics enhances the inverted U-shaped effect of rhetoric aesthetics and its indirect effect, whereas sleep space image aesthetics weakens both. Post-hoc analysis shows a positive direct effect of image aesthetics on customers' booking intentions. Supplementary analysis further indicates that rhetoric aesthetics linearly increases cognitive load, and that positive emotion is lowest at a low level of rhetoric aesthetics but does not differ significantly between medium and high levels. This study advances aesthetics research in P2P accommodation, deepens the understanding of the synergistic and antagonistic mechanisms of multimodal aesthetics, and provides decision support for hosts and platform managers to optimize multimodal aesthetic information to meet customers' aesthetic needs.

Title: Navigating AI-driven technological pressure: How top management team IT readiness and strategic orientation shape data breach risk
Authors: Niaz Mohammed, Chul Woo Yoo
Abstract: Rapid advances in artificial intelligence (AI) are reshaping industry practices and creating new security vulnerabilities, raising questions about the effectiveness of firms' internal risk management capabilities under heightened technological pressure. Drawing on socio-technical systems theory, we investigate how top management team (TMT) IT readiness influences firm-level data breach risk under the external technological pressure of industry AI exposure, and how firm strategic positioning shapes that response. Using a comprehensive firm-year panel dataset, we first confirm, consistent with prior research, that TMT IT readiness is associated with lower data breach risk. Building on this baseline, our central findings show that this effect is not uniform but is conditioned by the firm's technological and strategic context. The breach-reducing effect of TMT IT readiness becomes stronger in industries with higher AI exposure, and this moderating effect is itself contingent on firm strategic positioning. Specifically, the effect is more pronounced among innovation-oriented firms and less consistent among efficiency-oriented firms. These findings advance the data breach literature by identifying the boundary conditions of the well-established link between TMT IT readiness and breach risk, showing that its effectiveness amplifies under higher industry AI exposure and depends on firm strategic positioning. This study also offers practical implications for managers by highlighting the need to tailor security governance to industry-level technological pressures.

Title: Editorial Board
Beyond blind feature injection: An information foraging theory-guided deep learning framework for product recommendation
Authors: Weiyue Li, Ming Gao, Jingmin An, Bowei Chen, Jiafu Tang, Xuhui Wang, Yeming Gong
Abstract: Recommender systems significantly improve the quality and confidence of consumer decisions by alleviating information overload through streamlined retrieval, playing a vital role in e-commerce platforms. However, most recommender systems underutilize contextual information and fail to explicitly model users’ cognitive processes, leading to biased preference learning. Drawing on information foraging theory, this study adopts the design science research methodology to develop Tiresias, a framework that aligns with users’ cognitive processes by mimicking how proximal cues and foraging costs are assessed for each product. Proximal cues such as product category and affinitive relationships, and foraging costs such as behavior type, dwell time, and foraging progression, are identified and encoded as learnable features. To model the product-foraging journey, Typhon is designed as a Kolmogorov–Arnold network-enhanced differential transformer with a non-invasive feature injection mechanism. A multi-task learning objective that combines next-product prediction with auxiliary cue and cost prediction refines contextualized preference representations. Experiments on datasets show that Tiresias achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming baselines by up to 5.44%. Finally, post-hoc analysis reveals learned representation patterns consistent with dynamic preference evolution throughout the user’s product foraging journey. Methodologically, the study demonstrates how information foraging theory can guide feature selection, feature learning, and objective design. Practically, the study offers actionable insights for developing cognitive process-aware recommender systems that better support consumer decision-making.

Title: Designing satisfying AI-based work processes: The role of collaboration modality and task characteristics
Authors: Zi-Hao Wang, Xuan-Hua Xu, Yang-Yang Qian
Abstract: Although integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into work processes is often expected to enhance productivity, such transformation may also undermine employee satisfaction, which is essential for the long-term success of AI adoption. As organizations implement various modalities of human–AI collaboration, it remains unclear how these arrangements affect employee satisfaction. This paper addresses this gap by delineating three distinct collaboration modalities: human-led, AI-led, and co-led. We examine how each modality influences user satisfaction with collaborative outcomes and collaborative processes, and how these effects vary across task environments. Our findings show that when task uncertainty is low, the human-led modality leads to higher outcome satisfaction; however, as uncertainty increases, differences in outcome satisfaction across modalities diminish. In contrast, process satisfaction remains consistently sensitive to collaboration modality regardless of task uncertainty, and this effect is further amplified by task complexity. Across all conditions, the AI-led modality produces the highest levels of process satisfaction. Moreover, we also reveal a tension between satisfaction and performance. Although the co-led modality produces lower satisfaction with both the outcome and the process, it achieves the highest decision quality. By shifting attention from collaboration performance alone to collaboration satisfaction, this study extends research on human–AI collaboration and offers practical guidance for designing AI-based work processes that support both effectiveness and sustainability.

Title: Designing for persuasion: A theory-driven intent-aware explainable social recommendation system
Authors: Dongyang Li, Jianshan Sun, Kun Yuan, Jennifer Shang
Abstract: Social recommendation leverages users’ social network information to enhance product recommendation. To mitigate the issue of low-quality social signals, prior studies have introduced graph denoising and graph disentanglement. However, due to the lack of strong supervision, these methods often yield suboptimal performance. In this study, we propose a new framework for explicit semantic disentanglement. Specifically, we first use a Large Language Model (LLM) to extract user intentions from reviews and construct intention-specific collaborative subgraphs, which serve as supervision signals to disentangle the social graph into multiple intention-specific social subgraphs. This enables the model to independently learn interaction and social signals under different intentions. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and explainability.

Title: An investor demand-oriented approach for financial market segmentation based on network embedding techniques
Authors: Yan Liu, Wuyue Shangguan, Xi Chen, Alvin Chung Man Leung
Abstract: Financial market segmentation has predominantly relied on supply-based methods that emphasize the corporate business market, while paying scarce attention to demandoriented schemes that highlight shared investor preferences and behaviors. This study narrows this gap by proposing an investor demand-oriented approach for financial market segmentation, which consists of three fundamental phases: financial network construction based on investor co-attention, network representation learning using network embedding techniques, and clustering over network embeddings. By implementing the approach in the U.S. stock market and cross-validating its usefulness in the Chinese stock market, we first show that it can reflect pairwise stock similarity, as network embedding similarity is significantly and positively associated with excess comovement between stocks. We then partition the stock market into different peer groups that demonstrate significant within-group comovement. The utility and efficacy of our approach are comprehensively evaluated by comparing it with traditional industry classifications, geographical location-based classification, text-based classification, and search cluster-based investment habitats. The results demonstrate that our approach not only achieves better performance in capturing greater withingroup homogeneity and between-group heterogeneity, but also outperforms standard classification schemes in predicting excess comovement and stock returns. This study adds to design science research on financial market segmentation by extending the important yet underexplored domain of demand-oriented methods. By systematically decoding latent investor preferences and behavioral commonalities, our approach can be integrated into automated decision support systems to improve the accuracy and efficiency of financial market analytics pragmatically.

Title: A multimodal transfer learning framework for cross-project knowledge transfer to predict operation risk of complicated engineering machinery
Authors: Jin Xu, Xin Chen, Huiqi Zhao, Xin Li
Abstract: Operational risk plays a critical role in the management of construction projects. In particular, when complicated machinery is involved, failure to effectively monitor such risks can lead to severe accidents and project delays. Machine learning presents a promising solution to this engineering challenge. However, due to the inherent heterogeneity across construction projects, leveraging historical project data for risk prediction in target projects remains a significant challenge. In this study, we design a multimodal transfer learning framework to predict variations in engineering-machinery operations from plans. To select appropriate source projects for knowledge transfer, we consider both the similarity between source and target projects (built up on project management documentation and operational data) and the importance of source projects within the project similarity network. Our model also integrates multimodal information to strengthen its predictive capability. We evaluate our approach on real-world shield tunnel boring machine projects and demonstrate that the proposed framework significantly outperforms state-of-the-art models. Our results indicate that the framework serves as a practical and effective tool for improving the management of complex engineering projects.

Title: Immersive systems across extended reality: From technology categories to mechanism-centered explanation
Authors: Yixiu Yu, Andrew N.K. Chen
Abstract: Immersive technologies across extended reality (xR), including virtual reality, augmented reality, and mixed reality, are reshaping how individuals and organizations represent, experience, and act upon digital information. Yet information systems research on immersive technologies remains fragmented across technology categories, theoretical perspectives, application domains, and levels of analysis, limiting cumulative theory development. This study synthesizes 252 immersive-technology studies from leading IS journals and conferences to examine how this fragmented literature can be integrated. Our analysis reveals that, although prior studies appear diverse at the surface level, they increasingly converge around two interrelated analytical layers. First, higher-order mechanisms, including affordance-based, dynamic/temporal, tension-based, social/identity, and signal/data-driven mechanisms, shape how immersive environments structure, coordinate, constrain, balance, adapt, and personalize human–technology interaction across contexts and over time. Second, foundational experiential processes, including perceptual, cognitive, and affective processes, constitute the proximal pathways through which immersive systems influence environmental perception, information processing, emotional engagement, behavior, and outcomes. Building on these insights, we develop a mechanism-centered framework that reconceptualizes immersive systems not as isolated technology categories, but as configurations that generate nonlinear, contingent, and multi-level outcomes through the interaction of higher-order mechanisms and foundational experiential processes. By shifting the analytical focus from technology categories to mechanism-centered explanation, this study provides an integrated foundation for cumulative theory development and advances understanding of immersive systems as adaptive, experience-mediated information systems. We conclude by outlining a research agenda for future immersive systems research in IS and for the design of next-generation immersive decision support systems.

Title: From sparsity to precision: Enhancing bundle recommendations via large language model augmentation and Multi-Graph fusion
Authors: Yuanzhong Jiang, Kun Yuan, Jennifer Shang, Xi Chen, Yuanchun Jiang
Abstract: Bundle recommendation is a widely used marketing strategy designed to suggest related items to users, providing users with one-stop convenience while increasing platform efficiency. Yet, aligning bundle recommendations with user preferences remains challenging due to the complex tripartite relationships among users, bundles, and items. This challenge is further exacerbated by sparse user–bundle interactions, where the large number of bundles and limited user engagements hinder accurate preference estimation and often result in suboptimal outcomes. To address these issues, we propose an advanced multi-graph contrastive framework powered by large language models (LLMs). The framework integrates multi-view expansion and LLM-based data augmentation to enrich interaction signals, while employing multi-graph contrastive learning to improve the accuracy and robustness of representation learning. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across overall performance and varying sparsity conditions, underscoring its effectiveness across three benchmark real-world datasets. Moreover, the observed alignment between sparse and dense users with similar preferences suggests that the LLM-enhanced augmentation enables the model to learn meaningful representations even under sparse settings.

Title: How chatbot response features influence user adoption: A linguistic signaling perspective
Authors: Yusheng Zhou, Lei Zhu, Mingzhou Chen, Haoting Shen, Jia Yu
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-powered chatbots are becoming increasingly popular, with users engaging these chatbots to obtain information or to “socialize.” While previous research has considered the mechanisms governing user adoption of chatbots at a macro level, the underlying micro-level logic remains vague. Based on signal theory and dual-process theory, we propose a research model elucidating the signaling role of linguistic features in chatbot responses during user–chatbot interactions. Particularly, we focus on three linguistic signals: informative, affective, and matching signals, and investigate their impact on user adoption at the message level of interactions. The research model is empirically analyzed using chat logs collected from an online AI chat platform hosted in the United States that documents interactions between users and AI chatbots. According to the results, all three signals significantly influence users' adoption of chatbot responses—albeit with directionally variant effects. Furthermore, certain signals are moderated by user expertise and task complexity. Overall, this study both enriches our understanding of linguistic signals during human–AI interaction and affords practical insights regarding the improvement of AI chatbots.

Title: Two to tango: Physician linguistic style matching and patient revisits in online mental healthcare consultations
Authors: Yan Liu, Xingtong Chen, Zhijun Yan, Yang-Jun Li
Abstract: Effective mental healthcare typically evolves through an ongoing therapeutic process grounded in sustained physician-patient interactions, where patient revisits play a key role in maintaining such continuity. Nevertheless, empirical research on patient revisits in online mental healthcare settings remains limited. Drawing upon interpersonal trust theory, this study examines whether and how initial physician linguistic style matching (LSM) influences patient revisits in online mental healthcare consultations. Analyzing a large-scale dataset of over 227 thousand real-world consultations from a leading Chinese online healthcare platform, we find a robust, positive association between initial physician LSM and patient revisits. Bootstrapped mediation analysis suggests that this effect operates through a dual trust-building mechanism that fosters both patient affective and cognitive trust. We also observe suggestive evidence of a potential expectation-violation pattern, whereby the positive effect of physician LSM on patient cognitive trust may attenuate at very high levels. Further analyses show that the positive effect of physician LSM is more pronounced when physician responses are more topic-relevant and among patients with milder emotional distress. Finally, the observed effect persists among returning patients and those with chronic physical conditions (e.g., hypertension and diabetes), and physician LSM in publicly visible consultations also serves as a diagnostic signal influencing third-party patient selection. Collectively, our findings advance understanding of patient revisits, physician-patient interactions, and linguistic accommodation in online mental healthcare consultations and provide practical implications to promote effective, patient-centered healthcare.

Title: Corrigendum to ‘Designing AI-driven augmented living spaces with spatial augmented reality to support the autonomy of individuals with amnestic mild cognitive impairment’ [Decision support systems (2026) 114652]
Authors: Martin Böhmer, Stephan Kuehnel, Johannes Damarowsky
Abstract: The authors declare the following financial interests/personal relationships which may be considered as potential competing interests: Financial support was provided by the German Federal Ministry of Education and Research (grant number 03WIR3107B).Martin Böhmer: Writing – original draft, Writing – review & editing, Methodology, Conceptualization, Investigation, Formal analysis, Data curation, Visualization, Validation, Software, Resources, Project administration. Stephan Kuehnel: Writing – review & editing, Methodology, Conceptualization, Data curation, Visualization, Validation, Funding acquisition, Supervision. Johannes Damarowsky: Conceptualization, Funding acquisition, Supervision.

Title: Unveiling the hidden layer: Ambivalent cognitive effects of XAI in augmented decision-making under uncertainty
Authors: Tizian Matschak, Ilja Nastjuk, Simon Trang, Jose Benitez
Abstract: This study investigates whether explainable AI (XAI), although intended to improve calibrated reliance in augmented decision-making (ADM), may also increase negative consultations. In a between-subjects online experiment ( n = 200), participants completed a price classification task supported by AI, while we manipulated the presence of local feature-based explanations. Drawing on dual-process theory as an interpretive lens, we conceptualize explainability as a cognitively ambivalent intervention that reshapes reliance behavior. Our results show that XAI-induced transparency exerts competing effects: while it directly reduces negative consultations, it simultaneously increases competence-based trust and shifts responsibility attribution toward the AI. These mechanisms foster overreliance and significantly increase negative consultations, resulting in a competitive mediation pattern. Notably, comparable effects do not emerge for positive consultations, suggesting that transparency more readily amplifies reliance than it promotes corrective belief updating. By empirically demonstrating this paradox, our study develops IS and Decision Sciences research on automation bias in transparent ADM settings and identifies key psychological mechanisms through which explainability influences reliance. These findings inform the design of XAI systems that prioritize calibrated reliance rather than merely increasing perceived transparency.

Title: Stock time series prediction correction expert: A knowledge-guided stable multiple large language models enhancement method
Authors: Dingxiao Wang, Hongke Zhao, Likang Wu, Xinyu Li
Abstract: Stock prediction in financial markets aims to forecast stock trends and prices, which is crucial for achieving profitable investments. Traditional methods primarily involve modeling and predicting based on stock time-series data. Although many recent studies have incorporated contextual signals such as financial events, corporate disclosures, and investor sentiment, existing forecasting models often use such information mainly as predictive inputs rather than as evidence for post-hoc forecast correction. As a result, baseline forecasts may remain over-dependent on historical data distributions and become misaligned with current market conditions in uncertain decision-making processes. In contrast, large language models (LLMs), as decision models driven by rich knowledge, are powerful tools that can help us construct such correction mechanisms. We propose SPCE, a Post-Hoc Expert Correction framework decoupling trend extrapolation from causal reasoning. First, it adopts a correction-over-training paradigm where LLMs refine baseline forecasts without retraining. Second, a Knowledge-Guided mechanism mitigates forecast bias by grounding corrections in dynamic financial knowledge graphs and real-time sentiment. Third, a Regime-Adaptive Multi-Agent strategy orchestrates specialized LLMs, fusing their outputs via meta-cognitive consistency checks to ensure robust, context-aware predictions in volatile markets. Experiments conducted on three benchmark datasets, CMIN-US, StockNet, and CMIN-CN, show that SPCE achieves average reductions of 7.2% in RMSE, 8.9% in MAE, and 9.3% in MAPE compared with the CNN-BiLSTM-Attention baseline. The results highlight its effectiveness in volatile and heterogeneous market environments, positioning SPCE as a scalable and adaptable decision support mechanism for financial forecasting.

Title: Socializing online knowledge platforms: How social post features influence user knowledge contribution and mitigate the adverse impact of generative AI
Authors: Yuan Chen, Dongmei Han, Lifeng He, Yu Liu, Xiaohang Zhou
Abstract: Online knowledge platforms have become essential infrastructures for digital knowledge creation and exchange, yet sustaining user knowledge contributions remains a persistent challenge due to high cognitive demands and limited social incentives. This challenge has been further intensified by the widespread adoption of generative AI (GenAI). To address this issue, many platforms have introduced social post features that encourage informal, socially driven content sharing. This study investigates how social post features affect user knowledge contributions and whether they mitigate the adverse effects of GenAI. First, leveraging a large-scale panel dataset of over 10,000 user activity records, this study exploits the platform's rollout of the “idea” feature—a social post function—as an exogenous policy shock and employs a Difference-in-Differences (DID) approach within a quasi-experimental framework. The DID analysis results indicate that the introduction of social post features significantly increases knowledge contributions. Further analysis of the underlying mechanisms reveals that this effect operates primarily through enhanced self-disclosure, increased social interaction, and improved task decomposability. Furthermore, using an interrupted time-series analysis based on the release of ChatGPT as an exogenous GenAI shock, we find that while GenAI generally reduces user knowledge contributions, users who actively engage in social posts experience significantly smaller declines, indicating that socially oriented design features can effectively buffer the negative impacts of GenAI. Our findings offer theoretical insights and practical guidance for sustaining user engagement and maintaining resilient knowledge ecosystems in the GenAI era.

Title: Traditional, subscription, or data compensation: An economic analysis of optimal privacy protection models on ad-supported platforms
Authors: Nan Feng, Jianing Zhu, Wenyi Zhang, Haiyang Feng
Abstract: As privacy concerns intensify and data regulations become increasingly stringent, ad-supported platforms are adopting distinct privacy protection models to balance advertising revenue with consumers’ privacy expectations. This paper develops an analytical framework to compare three prevalent models: the traditional model, in which platforms unconditionally collect consumer data and expose users to advertisements; the subscription model, which offers users an opt-out option by paying a fee to avoid both data collection and advertising; and the data compensation model, which provides monetary incentives to users who voluntarily share their personal data. Our model specifically examines an ad-supported platform’s decisions regarding the optimal privacy protection model and data collection intensity for consumers exhibiting heterogeneous privacy sensitivity. Our analysis identifies the conditions under which each model becomes the platform’s profit-maximizing choice and examines how these choices impact social welfare and consumer surplus. We find that when the intensity of privacy infringement is high, the subscription model is optimal for the platform; whereas when the privacy infringement is low, the data compensation model yields the highest platform profits; otherwise, the traditional model outperforms the other models. Furthermore, while all three models can achieve maximum social welfare, only the data compensation model has the potential to create a win-win outcome for both the platform and consumers. In contrast, the subscription and traditional models often enhance platform profits at the expense of consumer welfare. These findings provide theoretical and policy insights for designing effective privacy strategies in content platforms.

Title: Augmenting machine learning with human knowledge for sentiment analysis of corporate disclosures
Authors: Ka Chung Ng, Jiexin Zheng, Rong Zheng
Abstract: We propose the Expert-Augmented Semantic Embedding (EASE) weighting scheme, which integrates domain knowledge into machine learning-based sentiment analysis of corporate disclosures. EASE leverages the Loughran and McDonald financial sentiment lexicon to geometrically define a semantically meaningful direction in a word embedding space, enabling continuous and graded sentiment scoring of the full lexicon, including words absent from the original lexicon, without requiring labeled outcome data or model retraining. Using a large sample of 10-K annual reports, we show that EASE-augmented sentiment measures exhibit improved economic significance and explanatory power for market returns and future earnings relative to their non-augmented counterparts. Because EASE anchors sentiment weights to an expert-defined semantic axis rather than to historically observed outcomes, the resulting measures are potentially less susceptible to the influence of strategically deployed or otherwise shifting language in corporate disclosures. Our findings highlight the complementarity between human knowledge and machine learning in extracting economically meaningful sentiment from financial texts.

Title: Guiding decisions in empirical research: A precision-driven app with context-specific criteria for confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling
Authors: Nadine Schröder, Andreas Falke, Herbert Endres
Abstract: The problem of assessing model misspecification and precision for decision making in areas such as business, cyber security, and medicine remains a pivotal issue. Current state-of-the-art methods in structural equation modeling rely on fixed fit criteria combinations and cut-offs, regardless of model or data characteristics. This approach is often questioned as variations in criteria often depend on these characteristics, raising doubts about the reliability of current decision-making processes and research insights. To address this limitation, we applied a precision-based approach to develop context-specific rules for model assessment and provide them in an easy-to-use Shiny App. This approach is crucial because high precision mitigates the risk of misleading or erroneous insights. Our context-specific rules represent a novel and relevant advancement in model evaluation. They are based on the insight that the performance of criteria combinations depends not only on the characteristics of the data and the model, but also on the specific class of structural equation model employed, such as confirmatory factor analysis or covariance-based structural equation modeling. As a result of our optimization, our developed rules have lower Type I error rates (with an average reduction of almost 50%) than state-of-the-art general combinations while keeping Type II error rates at a low level. Our Shiny App is designed to be user-friendly and accessible, requiring no prior expertise in simulation or programming. This precision-driven, adaptive approach aligns with the goals of decision support systems, which aim to provide context-sensitive insights to support informed, data-driven decisions.

Title: Crime dynamics of home-sharing: Disentangling temporal effects and policy interventions
Authors: Jiana Meng, He Li, Cheng Nie, Chen Zhang
Abstract: Despite its benefits, home-sharing has raised societal concerns about crime. However, research across disciplines has found inconsistent effects of home-sharing on crime. Regarding these inconsistencies, this research examines the temporal dynamics among home-sharing, long-term rental, and various types of crime. We also probe the moderating effects of the local government's short-term rental licensing regulation. We find that the prevalence of home-sharing has a direct positive association with crimes against property in the short term and with crimes against persons in the long term. Through the long-term rental price channel, however, the prevalence of home-sharing has a long-term effect on crimes, leading to higher levels of crimes against property but lower levels of crimes against persons. The licensing regulation mitigates home-sharing's direct adverse impacts on both types of crimes, but the effect becomes insignificant over time. This research contributes to a nuanced understanding of how home-sharing affects crime by delineating both direct effects and effects through the long-term rental channel, as well as their temporal distinctions. We offer practical implications for policymakers, platform operators, hosts, and local communities to promote safer and more sustainable governance of home-sharing.

Title: Configuring human and AI investments: Synergy and its impact on operational efficiency
Authors: Jiawei Xu, Baofeng Zhang, Jianjun Lu
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in the operations of firms. While prior research highlights the value of AI technologies, it often overlooks the collaborative role of humans in shaping firm operational outcomes. Drawing on a multi-source integrated dataset of Chinese firms, this study develops a firm-level measure of human–AI investment synergy and empirically examines its effect on firm operational efficiency. The results indicate that human–AI investment synergy enhances firm operational efficiency by promoting AI-driven innovation. This positive effect is stronger for firms with a more diversified customer base, suggesting that the value of human–AI investment synergy becomes more salient in information-intensive and heterogeneous task environments. The findings further reveal that different configurations of AI human and non-human investments are associated with heterogeneous operational outcomes. In particular, among firms with imbalanced AI resource allocation structures, those with relatively high AI-human and low AI non-human investment exhibit higher operational efficiency than comparable firms with the opposite configuration. Our findings deepen the understanding of the mechanisms through which human–AI collaboration shapes organizational operations and provide practical insights for managers regarding AI resource deployment decisions.

Title: Distinguishing good from bad in federated learning: A novel data fraud detection method using prototype learning and variational autoencoder
Authors: Zongxiang Zhang, Chenghong Zhang, Gang Chen, Shuaiyong Xiao, Lihua Huang
Abstract: Federated learning enables privacy-preserving collaborative modeling and has been widely adopted in data-driven decision-making scenarios such as financial risk management and healthcare analytics. However, its inherent characteristic of “data being available but not visible” introduces a critical vulnerability: malicious participants may manipulate local data or model updates to conduct fraud, thereby degrading model performance and undermining decision reliability. Addressing such fraud is particularly challenging due to limited data transparency, heterogeneous updates, and the lack of interpretable and robust detection mechanisms. To tackle these challenges, this study proposes a novel method, Distributed-Collaborative-Representation-Based Data Fraud Detection (DcrDFD). First, we develop a prototype learning-based representation construction mechanism that transforms participant updates into representative prototypes, enabling interpretable identification of normal, noisy, and fraudulent patterns. Second, we design a multi-variational autoencoder (VAE)-based mutual evaluation mechanism, where prototypes are collaboratively reconstructed and evaluated, significantly enhancing robustness against complex and dynamic data fraud. Third, we introduce a joint optimization framework that integrates fraud detection with federated learning training, enabling dynamic coordination between model learning and fraud prevention. Experiments on four real-world datasets demonstrate that DcrDFD outperforms state-of-the-art methods in model performance, fraud detection accuracy, and robustness, while maintaining a favorable balance between effectiveness and computational overhead. Overall, this study enhances interpretability, robustness, and reliability in federated learning, providing important implications for secure and trustworthy distributed decision support systems.

Title: Designing AI-based decision support systems for carbon stock estimation and planning: A design science research
Authors: Amelia S. Li, Shan L. Pan, Yenni Tim, Hoang D. Nguyen
Abstract: Mitigating climate change presents significant challenges, particularly in effective carbon stock estimation and planning. Decision-making based on quantified carbon stock is essential for enabling carbon sequestration efforts in natural ecosystems, yet traditional field measurements are labor-intensive, geographically constrained, and difficult to be adopted at scale. Motivated by this practical challenge, we undertook a design science research (DSR) project to develop AI-based decision support systems that enhance the efficiency, accessibility, and scalability for carbon stock estimation and planning. Guided by technology affordance theory, our iterative design, development, demonstration, and evaluation process has led to the conceptualization of four affordance-based design principles that build on and contribute to the growing design knowledge for environmental sustainability. This research advances our understanding of the critical problem and solution domains of carbon stock estimation and planning. It also facilitates the emerging discourse on balancing AI and human intelligence in designing systems for complex decision-making challenges for sustainability. This study provides an exemplar of DSR for supporting Sustainable Development Goal 13 by demonstrating how to design systems that facilitate carbon sequestration and societal transition toward environmental sustainability.

Title: Beyond Fog: Measuring managerial obfuscation using LLMs
Authors: Richard Zhe Wang
Abstract: This study develops a conceptual framework of semantic obfuscation in corporate disclosures and proposes a decision support system (DSS) built on large language models (LLMs) to operationalize it at scale. Four dimensions of managerial obfuscation are identified (vagueness, hedging, positive spin, and inconsistency) and scored across more than 16,000 Management Discussion and Analysis (MD&A) sections from U.S. 10-K filings. The LLM-derived measures are validated through multiple layers of evidence: the measures are highly reproducible across independent scoring runs, consistent with trained human judgments, empirically distinct from traditional readability and tone indices, and predictive of earnings management in theoretically expected directions. In an application to analyst forecasts, the semantic dimensions differentially predict forecast dispersion and accuracy where traditional readability indices do not. The framework advances financial DSS design by positioning generative LLMs as semantic scoring engines capable of transforming unstructured managerial narratives into structured, interpretable signals for analysts, investors, and regulators.

Title: Analyzing voluntary employee turnover: A data-driven explanatory modeling approach
Authors: Elisa Pöppel, Alexander Schiller, Lucas Weinfurtner
Abstract: A widespread shortage of skilled employees, which also includes the increasing difficulty to retain talented employees by limiting voluntary employee turnover, impedes company success. To gather insights on voluntary employee turnover, previous research has conducted explanatory research focused on theory-driven hypotheses, or utilized predictive models, aiming to predict which employees are most likely to leave the company based on historical data. In contrast, we propose a methodology that combines predictive data mining methods, causal decision trees, and an expert validation to yield firm-specific actionable explanations for employee turnover. The proposed methodology is applied to a real-world case of a mechanical engineering company. Here, our data-driven causal analysis identifies patterns of voluntary service technician turnover, which are validated by domain experts and used to derive targeted measures for reducing future employee turnover. The results are shown to provide valuable insights, adding to the a priori knowledge of the experts, revealing discrepancies between subjective opinions and quantitative results, and substantially informing the company's decision-making. A follow-up study demonstrates that almost all of the derived measures are being realized and indicates early positive effects on employee turnover.

Title: PFMAR: A multi-agent conversational recommender system for high-involvement products
Authors: Jianshan Sun, Wenjuan Chen, Chongming Gao, Ying Xue, Kun Yuan
Abstract: High-involvement product recommendation, due to its high value and high perceived risks, often leads to user preference shifts during multi-turn conversations, exacerbating issues such as the inherent instability of large language model (LLM)-based conversational recommender systems (CRS), thus posing challenges for existing CRS. To fill this research gap, we focus on high-involvement product recommendation scenario and develop a multi-agent recommender framework that integrates both reflection and critique. By designing a Reflector agent that reflects on user feedback at the user decision-making level, it promptly captures user preference instability and updates system strategies; by designing two Critic agents that monitor system responses in real-time, it mitigates the problem of unstable system generation. Overall, through multi-agent collaboration, the framework addresses the inherent user preference instability in this scenario. Experiments on a real-world product dataset from the automotive domain demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Furthermore, additional experiments show that in scenarios characterized by severe preference instability, our model still achieves higher recommendation accuracy, while in scenarios with stable user preferences, it can complete recommendations in fewer dialogue turns. Its effectiveness in the high-involvement product recommendation scenario demonstrates its practical application potential.

Title: How to initiate human-agent intervention for recovery when chatbots fail: A social information processing perspective
Authors: Zhenzhen Lu, Jiahui Mo, Xin (Robert) Luo, Qingfei Min
Abstract: Service failures are inevitable in chatbot-based customer service. In hybrid customer service systems, when a chatbot fails, a human agent typically takes over and resume service for the customer. However, little is known about how to effectively initiate this transition from chatbot failure to human-agent intervention. This study identifies four initiation methods varying in service proactivity: passive initiation, text prompt initiation, button prompt initiation, and automatic initiation. Extending social information processing theory with a cognitive decision perspective, we develop a theoretical framework to examine how consumers attribute the observed initiation methods to organizational motives, which subsequently influence their satisfaction. We conduct three online experiments to examine how these initiation methods influence recovery satisfaction, as well as the underlying psychological mechanisms and boundary conditions. The results reveal significant differences in recovery satisfaction across initiation methods, mediated by customers' inferred selfish intent. Furthermore, compared with low task urgency, high task urgency significantly amplifies differences in recovery satisfaction and inferred selfish intent among various human-agent initiation methods. These findings advance understanding of recovery strategies for chatbot service failures, offering actionable guidance for designing effective transitions from chatbots to human agents in hybrid service settings.

Title: Beyond interlocks: Board networks and corporate social responsibility performance similarity
Authors: Qin Su, Yue Fang, Zhe Zhang, Xin Bao, Raymond Y.K. Lau
Abstract: While firms largely rely on inter-organizational information and resources to make corporate social responsibility (CSR) decisions, very few studies have delved into the heterogeneous effects of different categories of board networks. Through adopting a large language model (LLM) as an analytical tool to transform unstructured resumes into structured decision-relevant intelligence, we fulfill this research gap by constructing in-depth board networks with three distinct types: current network, past network, and non-profit organization network. Based on a dataset of Chinese listed firms from 2011 to 2020, we empirically estimate whether and how firms connected through board networks would result in CSR performance similarity. The results show that the existence and heterogeneity of board networks are positively associated with CSR performance similarity between interlocked firms. Interestingly, our findings reveal that other than current networks, past networks, and non-profit networks have a higher impact on the CSR performance similarity. Further analysis suggests that the positive association between social networks and CSR performance similarity is attenuated when connected firms face higher media coverage and higher analyst coverage. Overall, this study provides insightful evidence to leverage the effect of board networks, informing decision support for investors, regulators, and corporate strategists by revealing hidden network drivers of CSR-related decisions.

Title: DISCO: Decoupling representation learning and risk control for reliable credit card fraud detection
Authors: Ruonan Zhu, Xinru Zhang, Tao Wang, Jingxiao Liao, Sai-Ho Chung, Xiaoge Zhang
Abstract: Credit card fraud detection remains a significant challenge due to extreme class imbalance, evolving fraud patterns, and asymmetric costs of misclassification. While existing machine learning methods often prioritize fraud detection performance, they frequently overlook model risk management, which is crucial for reliable decision making in high-stakes environments. To address this issue, we introduce DISCO—a framework that combines discriminative and robust representation learning with a conformal prediction-based mechanism for provable risk control. At its core, DISCO is established upon the principle of decoupling representation learning from risk-controlled decision-making. To this end, we first leverage deep metric learning (DML) to construct an embedding space that is inherently robust to class imbalance and resilient to concept drift. Subsequently, we employ a conformal risk control (CRC) mechanism to provide a formal statistical guarantee on the false negative rate (FNR) of the resulting model according to a user-specified FNR target. Computational experiments on a real-world dataset demonstrate that DISCO outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both classification performance and operational efficiency. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to integrate a DML-based representation learning with a formal risk control mechanism for reliable credit card fraud detection. The proposed framework therefore offers a trustworthy and practical solution that addresses the dual imperatives of predictive performance and reliability.

Title: The impact of multi-aspect electronic word-of-mouth on movie box office: An exploration study based on large language models
Authors: Liting Li, Yao He, Ling Liu, Jing Zhao
Abstract: Electronic word-of-mouth (eWOM) plays a critical role in shaping consumer decisions and influencing product sales. While prior research has extensively examined the relationship between aggregate eWOM metrics, such as valence and volume, and sales, less is known about how aspect-level eWOM sentiment relates to overall ratings and market outcomes. This study leverages large language models (LLMs) to extract fine-grained aspect-specific sentiment from online reviews and examines the relationships among multi-aspect sentiment, overall ratings, and product sales. Using data from the movie industry, we develop an LLM-based framework to identify sentiment toward plot, cast, director, and audiovisual, and empirically test their associations with ratings and box office using ridge regression. The findings show that plot sentiment has the strongest positive association with box office, followed by cast and director sentiment. Audiovisual sentiment is positively associated with overall ratings, but its relationship with box office is more context-dependent. Overall ratings partially mediate the effects of plot, cast, and director sentiment, and overall ratings, sentiment dispersion, and cross-aspect sentiment interactions further condition aspect-level effects. This research contributes to the eWOM literature by offering a fine-grained understanding of how multi-aspect sentiment relates to market outcomes and provides practical insights for managing online movie reputation.

Title: SMSF: A signal-driven multimodal sequence fusion framework for sales prediction in short-form video commerce
Authors: Xingpeng Xu, Xiapu Liu, Qingfeng Zeng, Songqiao Han, Weiguo Fan
Abstract: The rapid rise of short-form video commerce has posed new challenges for accurate sales prediction. Previous studies often overlook the sequential features and temporal structure of modality-specific data. Our main contribution is to develop a signal-driven multimodal sequence fusion (SMSF) framework grounded in signaling theory. SMSF employs a hierarchical attention-based fusion strategy that combines self-attention, pairwise cross-modal attention, and joint attention to enhance sequential modeling and enable effective representation of complex and heterogeneous multimodal signals beyond conventional fusion methods. All enhanced signals are fused via dynamic gating for adaptive modality selection, followed by a Mixture-of-Experts module that improves semantic coordination. We use a multimodal dataset of 8084 short-form sales videos from Douyin (TikTok in China) for experiments. The results indicate that SMSF consistently outperforms benchmark models. Ablation experiments further reveal that online comments contribute most to prediction performance. Its signal processing and enhancement methods provide a potential paradigm for multimodal tasks across different scenarios or platforms.

Title: Editorial Board
EGIVE (Efficient Global Interaction and Variable Explainability): A fast and comprehensive method for global interpretability analysis of black-box models
Authors: Matt Baucum, Meysam Rabiee, Babak Aslani, Kaushik Dutta
Abstract: Model interpretability is increasingly regarded as a core tenet of responsible data science. While there is a growing focus on inherently interpretable ML models, there is still a need for model-agnostic techniques that provide interpretable insights into already-trained ML models. This is particularly important for global interpretability analysis, which characterizes variable effects and interactions across the entire training set. However, existing global interpretability techniques often suffer from long runtimes, model dependence, and a lack of comprehensive and easy-to-implement frameworks. To address this gap, we propose EGIVE (Efficient Global Interaction and Variable Explainability), a framework which allows users to explore a full suite of efficiently-estimated interpretability metrics and visualizations. EGIVE provides importance scores and partial dependence visualizations for single-feature effects, pairwise interactions, and a user-defined set of three-way interactions. By reusing partial-dependence computations and partial dependence inverse propensity weighting to estimate interaction effects EGIVE achieves faster runtimes than baseline implementations in our benchmarks. We demonstrate EGIVE’s ability to recover ground-truth variable effects and interactions in simulated data, and we demonstrate EGIVE’s ability to quickly uncover meaningful clinical patterns using two real-world healthcare datasets.

Title: Differential impact of evaluative vs. non-evaluative AI feedback on employee safety performance and affective wellbeing
Authors: Chaorui Shen, Long Ye, Ye Yang, Ming Guo, Songlin Yang
Abstract: In safety-sensitive industries, AI feedback is increasingly being applied to employee decision-making and performance management. However, existing research has paid limited attention to differences in the institutional embedding of AI feedback and its contextual characteristics, making it difficult to fully understand its application effectiveness. To address these gaps, this study distinguishes between evaluative and non-evaluative AI feedback and introduces the concept of publicness of AI feedback.
